entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Han Dynasty (漢朝, Hàn Cháo), ruling China from 206 BCE to 220 CE (with a brief interruption by Wang Mang's Xin Dynasty 9-23 CE) — is one of the most significant dynasties in Chinese history, establishing the model of Chinese governance, culture, and identity that has defined China ever since: the Han people (汉族, Hànzú) — the ethnic designation of 92% of China's 1.4 billion people today — take their name from this dynasty, indicating its foundational role in Chinese civilization.

Han governance achievements were foundational: Emperor Wu (r. 141-87 BCE) institutionalized Confucianism as state philosophy (creating the civil service examination system's predecessor), expanded China's territory through military campaigns to Korea, Central Asia, and Vietnam, established the Silk Road trade networks with Rome and Parthia, and created the Han empire covering approximately 6 million square kilometers. Ban Zhao (45-116 CE) was one of history's earliest known female historians. Sima Qian (c.145-90 BCE) wrote the Shiji (Records of the Grand Historian), the foundational work of Chinese historical tradition.

Han China's trade connections reached the Roman Empire: archaeological evidence and Roman historical sources document silk imports from China ('the land of Seres'), and diplomatic missions may have reached Rome. The Silk Road under Han patronage was one of history's most consequential trade networks, spreading Buddhism (which entered China in this period), silk technology, and eventually facilitating the transmission of Chinese inventions westward.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Han Dynasty — whose name designates 92% of China's population, who institutionalized Confucianism, established the Silk Road, and created the model of Chinese governance — is one of history's most consequential dynasties and the foundational period of Chinese civilizational identity.
